definition: having or showing a wish to harm others

examples.text: The malevolent stepmother sends the children into the forest at dusk.
Villagers blamed the failed harvest on a malevolent spirit.
My brother gave me a malevolent grin just before the water balloon hit.

confused.note: Malevolent means wishing harm; benevolent means wishing good.

questions.passage: In most versions of the tale the forest witch is purely ______, luring travelers to their doom for her own amusement. This retelling makes her a healer whom frightened villagers have misunderstood.
questions.explanation: Luring travelers to their doom for amusement shows a wish to harm.

distractors.why: Benevolent means kindly, which describes the witch only in the retelling.
Timorous means fearful, which does not describe someone who lures travelers to their doom.
Nonchalant means casually unconcerned, which does not capture a wish to harm.

definition: to make something more noticeable

examples.text: The dye accentuates the cell walls so they show clearly under the microscope.
Short sentences accentuate the narrator's panic.
The dark frame accentuates the bright colors in the painting.

confused.note: Accentuate means to emphasize; accelerate means to speed up.

questions.passage: The stage designer hung plain black curtains behind the dancers. The dark background was meant to ______ their white costumes, making every movement stand out sharply.
questions.explanation: A dark background makes white costumes more noticeable.

distractors.why: Diminish means to make smaller or less, the opposite of making costumes stand out.
Parody means to imitate mockingly, which a curtain cannot do.
Berate means to scold, which does not fit.

partsNote: from Latin cantus, "song": to add tone to

definition: impossible to change or take back

examples.text: Crossing the river was an irrevocable step toward civil war.
She drops the letter in the box and knows at once that the act is irrevocable.
Hitting "send" on that text felt irrevocable.

confused.note: Irrevocable means unable to be undone; irrelevant means beside the point.

questions.passage: Applicants are warned that the decision is ______. Once a student accepts a place under the early program, the acceptance cannot be withdrawn, and all other applications are cancelled.
questions.explanation: An acceptance that cannot be withdrawn cannot be undone.

distractors.why: Trivial means unimportant, which a binding decision is not.
Ostensible means apparent but perhaps not real, which does not fit.
Tedious means boring, which is not the warning.

partsNote: not able to be called back

definition: calm and relaxed, as if not worried or interested

examples.text: The spy gives a nonchalant shrug while his heart pounds.
The pilot's nonchalant account made the crash landing sound like a picnic.
She tried to look nonchalant as she walked past the scholarship list.

confused.note: Nonchalant is the adjective; nonchalance is the noun.

questions.passage: The other finalists paced, bit their nails, and rehearsed under their breath. Only Imani appeared ______, leaning against the wall with her hands in her pockets as if waiting for a bus.
questions.explanation: Leaning casually while others fret shows a calm, unworried manner.

distractors.why: Timorous means fearful, which describes the other finalists.
Vehement means intense and forceful, the opposite of her relaxed pose.
Pugnacious means eager to fight, which she is not.

partsNote: from Latin calere, "to be warm": not heated

definition: knowing or seeming to know what will happen in the future

examples.text: Her prescient warning about the levees was ignored until the flood.
The 1970 paper was prescient in predicting how fast computers would shrink.
Bringing a spare charger turned out to be prescient.

confused.note: Prescient means foreseeing; it is unrelated to being present.

questions.passage: The novel, published in 1909, now seems remarkably ______. It describes a world in which people live alone in small rooms, communicate only through screens, and fear meeting one another face to face.
questions.explanation: A 1909 book describing life through screens seems to have foreseen the future.

distractors.why: Quixotic means idealistic and impractical, which does not describe accurate foresight.
Tedious means boring, which is not the point.
Abject means wretched or hopeless, which does not fit.

definition: extremely happy because of a success

examples.text: Jubilant crowds filled the square when the war ended.
The jubilant bridegroom dances with every guest.
We were jubilant when the snow day was announced.

confused.note: Jubilant means joyful; a jubilee is a special anniversary celebration.

questions.passage: When the final whistle confirmed the school's first championship in fifty years, the players were ______. They leapt into one another's arms, and several ran a lap of the field carrying the coach on their shoulders.
questions.explanation: Leaping, embracing, and carrying the coach show great joy at a success.

distractors.why: Abject means utterly miserable, the opposite of their mood.
Nonchalant means casually calm, which this celebration was not.
Imperious means bossy, which does not fit.

partsNote: from Latin jubilare, "to shout for joy"

definition: to stop resisting and give in

examples.text: After a six-month siege, the starving city capitulated.
The stubborn aunt finally capitulates and lets the lovers marry.
I capitulated to my sister's demand for the front seat after ten minutes of arguing.

confused.note: Capitulate means to give in; recapitulate means to summarize.

questions.passage: The union had vowed never to accept a pay cut. After eight weeks without wages, however, its members voted to ______, agreeing to the company's terms in exchange for a promise of no layoffs.
questions.explanation: Accepting terms they had vowed to refuse is giving in.

distractors.why: Balk means to refuse to go on, which is what they stopped doing.
Ruminate means to think deeply, which is not what the vote did.
Transgress means to break a rule, which does not fit.

partsNote: from Latin capitulum, "chapter": to agree to the terms listed

definition: appearing or claimed to be true, but possibly not true

examples.text: The ostensible purpose of the voyage was trade; the real one was to map the coast for an invasion.
The ostensible hero of the novel turns out to be its villain.
The ostensible reason for the meeting was planning, but mostly we ate donuts.

confused.note: Ostensible means apparent but perhaps not real; ostentatious means showy.

questions.passage: The ______ reason for the minister's visit was to open a new school. Reporters suspected that his true aim was to meet quietly with the region's governor, with whom he had long been at odds.
questions.explanation: The stated reason is contrasted with a suspected true aim.

distractors.why: Exhaustive means thorough, which does not describe a reason.
Jubilant means joyful, which does not fit.
Irrevocable means unable to be undone, which does not fit.

definition: to scold or criticize someone angrily

examples.text: The cook berates the kitchen boy for letting the sauce burn.
The general berated his officers in front of the entire army.
The coach berated us for showing up late to the bus.

confused.note: Berate means to scold angrily; it is unrelated to rating something.

questions.passage: The conductor was known for his temper. During one rehearsal he stopped the orchestra to ______ the brass section, shouting for five minutes that they were playing like "a herd of buffalo."
questions.explanation: Shouting insults for five minutes is angry scolding.

distractors.why: Nurture means to care for and encourage, the opposite of this outburst.
Accentuate means to emphasize, which does not fit.
Capitulate means to surrender, and it cannot take "the brass section" as an object.

definition: sharp and direct in a way that is critical or unkind

examples.text: The critic's acerbic reviews were more entertaining than most of the plays.
The senator was famous for acerbic remarks about his own party.
My sister's acerbic comment about my haircut was accurate, which made it worse.

confused.note: Acerbic describes sharp speech or wit; acidic describes a chemical property or sour taste.

questions.passage: The columnist's wit was ______. Of a rival's nine-hundred-page novel she wrote that it was "a book one puts down with great relief and cannot be persuaded to pick up again."
questions.explanation: A witty but cutting insult is sharp and critical.

distractors.why: Tedious means boring, which describes the novel she mocked, not her wit.
Timorous means timid, which this bold insult is not.
Exemplary means serving as a model, which is not how her wit is characterized.

definition: to think carefully and deeply about something

examples.text: The old captain ruminates on the choices that brought him to this shore.
The president ruminated for weeks before signing the order.
I ruminated on the test all weekend, replaying the one question I missed.

confused.note: Ruminate means to think deeply; terminate means to end.

questions.passage: The philosopher did not answer quickly. He liked to ______ on a question for days, turning it over during long walks, before he would commit a single sentence to paper.
questions.explanation: Turning a question over for days is thinking deeply.

distractors.why: Balk means to refuse or hesitate, which does not fit "on a question for days."
Capitulate means to surrender, which does not fit.
Berate means to scold, which does not fit.

partsNote: from Latin rumen, a cow's stomach: to chew over

definition: eager to argue or fight

examples.text: The pugnacious sailor challenges anyone who looks at him twice.
The pugnacious senator once started three duels in a single year.
Our pugnacious rooster attacks the mail carrier's boots.

confused.note: Pugnacious means eager to fight; pungent means sharp in smell or taste.

questions.passage: Even as a child the boxer was ______. Teachers recalled that he would argue about anything, from the rules of marbles to the spelling of his own name, and that the arguments often ended with fists.
questions.explanation: Arguing about everything and ending with fists shows eagerness to fight.

distractors.why: Timorous means timid and fearful, the opposite of this child.
Nonchalant means calm and unconcerned, which he was not.
Prescient means foreseeing the future, which is unrelated.

definition: easily frightened; nervous and lacking confidence

examples.text: The timorous clerk hides behind the ledger whenever the owner shouts.
Timorous advisers urged the queen to pay the ransom.
The timorous kitten spent its first day under the couch.

confused.note: Timorous means fearful; timely means happening at a good time.

questions.passage: The deer in the park have grown used to visitors and will eat from an open hand. Their wild cousins are far more ______, bolting into the trees at the snap of a twig a hundred meters away.
questions.explanation: Bolting at a distant sound shows they are easily frightened.

distractors.why: Pugnacious means eager to fight, the opposite of fleeing.
Jubilant means joyful, which does not fit.
Imperious means domineering, which does not describe frightened deer.

definition: a piece of writing, music, or acting that imitates a style in a funny, exaggerated way

examples.text: The poem is a parody of epic verse, with a kitten as its hero.
Cartoonists drew a parody of the king's portrait, giving him a pear for a head.
Our talent show act was a parody of a cooking program, with glue for frosting.

confused.note: A parody imitates a particular style for laughs; a satire uses humor to criticize people or society.

questions.passage: The film is not a serious western but a ______ of one. Its hero cannot ride a horse, its villain keeps forgetting his own threats, and the final showdown is postponed because of light rain.
questions.explanation: Exaggerated, comic imitation of a western is a parody.

distractors.why: A disparity is a large difference, which does not fit.
A catalyst is something that causes change, which does not fit.
A propensity is a tendency, which does not fit.

definition: of little importance or value

examples.text: The difference between the two samples was trivial and could be ignored.
The war began over a trivial insult at a banquet.
Do not waste the teacher's time with trivial questions about the font.

confused.note: Trivial is the adjective; a trifle is a thing of little importance.

questions.passage: The two researchers agreed on every major point. Their only disagreements were ______, concerning such matters as whether a chart should be printed in blue or green.
questions.explanation: A dispute over chart colors is of little importance.

distractors.why: Vehement means forceful and passionate, which is not shown by the example.
Irrevocable means unable to be undone, which does not fit.
Exhaustive means thorough, which does not describe a disagreement.

definition: boring and continuing for too long

examples.text: Counting pollen grains under a microscope is tedious but necessary work.
The tedious sermon sends half the congregation to sleep.
Copying the vocabulary list by hand was tedious.

confused.note: Tedious means boring; tenuous means weak or thin.

questions.passage: Before computers, calculating a comet's orbit was a ______ business. A team of clerks might spend three months on arithmetic, checking each column of figures twice, to produce a single prediction.
questions.explanation: Months of repetitive arithmetic is long and boring work.

distractors.why: Trivial means unimportant, but the prediction mattered.
Jubilant means joyful, which does not describe months of arithmetic.
Quixotic means impractically idealistic, but the work did produce results.

definition: a great difference, especially an unfair one

examples.text: The study found a wide disparity in air quality between the two neighborhoods.
The disparity between the nobles' wealth and the peasants' hunger fueled the revolt.
There is a disparity between how long my chores take and how long my brother's do.

confused.note: A disparity is a large difference between groups; a discrepancy is a mismatch between things that should agree.

questions.passage: The report draws attention to a striking ______ in funding. Schools in the northern district receive almost twice as much money per student as schools in the south, though both serve similar numbers of children.
questions.explanation: Twice the funding for similar schools is a great and unfair difference.

distractors.why: Parity means equality, the opposite of what the report found.
A propensity is a tendency, which does not fit.
A parody is a comic imitation, which does not fit.

definition: so good that it serves as a model for others

examples.text: The nurse was decorated for exemplary courage during the epidemic.
The lab's exemplary record keeping made the audit easy.
Her exemplary attendance earned her the last locker by the door.

confused.note: Exemplary is the adjective meaning model; exemplify is the verb meaning to be an example of.

questions.passage: The inspector found nothing to criticize. On the contrary, she described the kitchen's cleanliness as ______ and recommended that other restaurants in the city send their managers to observe it.
questions.explanation: A kitchen others should come to observe is a model.

distractors.why: Abject means wretched or of the lowest kind, the opposite of her praise.
Ostensible means apparent but doubtful, which would undercut her recommendation.
Pugnacious means eager to fight, which does not fit.

definition: to care for and encourage the growth of someone or something

examples.text: Penguins nurture a single chick through the Antarctic winter.
The academy nurtured two generations of the nation's painters.
My teacher nurtured my interest in astronomy by lending me her telescope.

confused.note: Nurture is care and upbringing; nature is what one is born with.

questions.passage: The editor did more than correct the young writer's grammar. Over ten years she ______ his talent, suggesting books to read, pushing him to revise, and defending his early work to doubtful publishers.
questions.explanation: Guiding and defending him over years is encouraging growth.

distractors.why: Squandered means wasted, the opposite of developing a talent.
Berated means scolded angrily, which is not what she did.
Parodied means imitated mockingly, which does not fit.

definition: including everything; complete and thorough

examples.text: The team carried out an exhaustive search of the genome for the mutation.
After an exhaustive study of the archives, she found the missing treaty.
I made an exhaustive list of everything I needed for the camping trip.

confused.note: Exhaustive means thorough; exhausting means very tiring.

questions.passage: The catalog is nothing if not ______. It lists every one of the painter's four thousand known works, including sketches on napkins, with the date, size, and current owner of each.
questions.explanation: Listing all four thousand works, even napkin sketches, is complete and thorough.

distractors.why: Trivial means unimportant, which is not what the examples show.
Acerbic means sharp and critical, which does not describe a catalog.
Timorous means fearful, which does not fit.

partsNote: from Latin haurire, "to drain": drained out

definition: extremely bad or severe; without hope or dignity

examples.text: The refugees lived in abject poverty in camps along the border.
He offers an abject apology on his knees.
My first attempt at baking bread was an abject failure.

confused.note: Abject means wretched; an object is a thing.

questions.passage: The expedition was not a partial success, as its sponsors later claimed. It was an ______ failure: the ships never left the harbor, the funds were lost, and the leader fled the country.
questions.explanation: Ships that never sailed and lost funds make the failure total and humiliating.

distractors.why: Exemplary means serving as a model, which this expedition was not.
Ostensible means apparent but perhaps not real; this failure was real.
Nonchalant means casually calm, which does not describe a failure.

definition: to be unwilling to do something or to let it happen

examples.text: The assembly balked at funding another war.
The mule balks at the bridge, and no amount of pulling will move it.
I balked at paying eight dollars for a small popcorn.

confused.note: Balk means to refuse or hesitate; bulk means large size.

questions.passage: Customers were happy to pay for faster delivery. They ______, however, when the company proposed charging an additional fee simply for the right to return unwanted goods.
questions.explanation: "However" signals that customers were unwilling to accept the new fee.

distractors.why: Capitulated means gave in, the opposite of refusing.
Ruminated means thought deeply, which does not capture their refusal.
Accentuated means emphasized, which does not fit.

definition: having ideas or plans that are noble but not practical

examples.text: The knight's quixotic quest to right every wrong ends in a ditch.
The duke's quixotic plan to drain the entire marsh bankrupted him.
My quixotic attempt to read every book in the library stalled in the A section.

confused.note: Quixotic means nobly impractical; exotic means strikingly foreign.

questions.passage: Friends admired the teacher's dream of building a free library in every village of the province. They also thought it ______: she had no funds, no staff, and a salary that barely covered her rent.
questions.explanation: A noble dream with no means to achieve it is idealistic and impractical.

distractors.why: Trivial means unimportant, but friends admired the dream.
Malevolent means wishing harm, the opposite of her generous aim.
Prescient means foreseeing the future, which is not the friends' concern.

partsNote: from Don Quixote, the knight of Cervantes's novel

definition: expecting to be obeyed; arrogant and commanding

examples.text: With an imperious wave, the duchess dismisses the musicians.
The governor's imperious manner united the colonists against him.
My cat gives an imperious meow at exactly six every morning.

confused.note: Imperious means bossy and arrogant; imperial means relating to an empire.

questions.passage: The chef ran her kitchen in an ______ manner. She did not ask but ordered, never explained a decision, and expected every instruction to be carried out before she had finished speaking.
questions.explanation: Ordering without explanation and demanding instant obedience is arrogant command.

distractors.why: Timorous means timid, the opposite of her manner.
Nonchalant means casually unconcerned, but she demanded instant obedience.
Jubilant means joyful, which does not fit.

definition: showing very strong feeling, especially anger or insistence

examples.text: Despite vehement protests from the merchants, the port was closed.
Her vehement denial only deepens the detective's suspicion.
My brother was vehement that he had not eaten the last waffle.

confused.note: Vehement means forceful in feeling or expression; violent involves physical force.

questions.passage: The proposal to close the village school met with ______ opposition. Parents filled the hall, several speakers were in tears, and one grandmother vowed to sit on the school steps until the plan was withdrawn.
questions.explanation: Tears, a packed hall, and a vow to protest show very strong feeling.

distractors.why: Nonchalant means unconcerned, the opposite of this reaction.
Trivial means unimportant, but the opposition was intense.
Ostensible means apparent but possibly not real; this opposition was plainly real.

definition: too elaborate or decorated; or red in the face

examples.text: The letter's florid compliments run on for a full page before reaching the point.
The palace's florid ceilings drip with gilded cherubs and plaster fruit.
The menu's florid description of a grilled cheese made me laugh.

confused.note: Florid means overly ornate; fluid means flowing.

questions.passage: The young poet's early verses were ______, crowded with roses, moonbeams, and sighing nightingales. Her later work is strikingly bare, sometimes a dozen plain words on an otherwise empty page.
questions.explanation: Verses crowded with roses and nightingales are overly decorated.

distractors.why: Sparse means thin and spare, which describes her later work.
Rigorous means strict and exact, which is not the contrast with "bare."
Defunct means no longer existing, which does not fit.

definition: to break a law or moral rule; to go beyond a limit

examples.text: Any merchant who transgressed the guild's rules lost his license.
The hero knows he has transgressed, and the guilt follows him across three continents.
I transgressed the unwritten rule of the group chat by replying "k."

confused.note: To transgress is to break a rule or limit; to transcend is to rise above a limit.

questions.passage: The monastery's code was strict, and those who ______ it could expect no leniency. A monk who spoke during the hours of silence, for instance, ate alone for a week.
questions.explanation: Breaking the code by speaking is violating a rule.

distractors.why: Renounced means formally gave up; the monks broke a rule, they did not abandon the code.
Cultivated means developed carefully, which does not fit.
Conveyed means communicated, which does not fit.

definition: a natural tendency to behave in a particular way

examples.text: The metal has a propensity to rust in salt air.
The narrator admits a propensity for exaggeration, so readers must judge his tales carefully.
My dog has a propensity for stealing socks.

confused.note: A propensity is a tendency; a proportion is a share or ratio.

questions.passage: Economists once assumed that people always act in their own financial interest. Later research revealed a widespread ______ to do the opposite, as when shoppers drive across town to save five dollars but ignore a fifty-dollar saving on a larger purchase.
questions.explanation: A widespread pattern of behavior is a tendency.

distractors.why: Contempt means scorn, which does not fit "to do the opposite."
A catalyst is something that triggers change, not a tendency.
A disparity is a gap between things, which does not fit.

definition: to become or make something smaller, weaker, or less important

examples.text: The drug's effect diminishes after six hours.
The loss of its colonies diminished the kingdom's influence.
A bad grade on one quiz does not diminish a whole semester of work.

confused.note: To diminish is to make smaller; to demolish is to destroy completely.

questions.passage: The star's brightness did not vanish all at once. It ______ gradually over several weeks, until it could be seen only through the observatory's largest telescope.
questions.explanation: Becoming gradually fainter is lessening.

distractors.why: Cultivated means nurtured, which does not describe fading light.
Subverted means undermined from within, which does not fit.
Exerted means applied force, which does not fit.

definition: to formally give up a claim, belief, or right

examples.text: The prince renounced his claim to the throne in order to marry a commoner.
She renounces her fortune and goes to work in the mill.
I have renounced soda, at least until the weekend.

confused.note: To renounce is to give something up; to denounce is to condemn it publicly.

questions.passage: To become a citizen of the new republic, an immigrant had to ______ all loyalty to any foreign king. The oath, taken before a judge, was regarded as binding for life.
questions.explanation: Formally giving up loyalty to a king is renouncing it.

distractors.why: Denounce means to condemn publicly; the oath required giving up loyalty, not attacking it.
Cultivate means to develop, the opposite of giving up.
Exploit means to make use of, which does not fit.

definition: making it easy or likely for something to happen

examples.text: Warm, shallow seas are conducive to the growth of coral.
Peace along the frontier was conducive to trade.
A noisy cafeteria is not conducive to studying.

confused.note: Conducive means helping to bring about; conductive means able to carry heat or electricity.

questions.passage: The library's new reading room was designed to be ______ to concentration. Its walls absorb sound, its lamps cast no glare, and its desks are spaced so that no reader can see another's screen.
questions.explanation: Quiet walls, soft light, and private desks make concentration easier.

distractors.why: Detrimental means harmful, the opposite of what the design intends.
Dispassionate means unemotional, which does not complete "to concentration."
Defunct means no longer in existence, which does not fit.

definition: to produce something; or to give way to pressure or to someone else

examples.text: The new variety of wheat yields a third more grain per field.
The fortress yielded only after its wells ran dry.
Drivers must yield to people in the crosswalk.

confused.note: To yield is to produce or give way; to wield is to hold and use a tool or power.

questions.passage: Decades of digging at the site had turned up little of interest. The latest season, by contrast, ______ a remarkable find: a sealed chamber containing forty painted jars.
questions.explanation: The digging produced a find.

distractors.why: Squandered means wasted, which does not describe turning up a discovery.
Subverted means undermined, which does not fit.
Entailed means involved as a necessary part, which does not capture producing a result.

definition: able to work successfully; capable of surviving

examples.text: Only a few of the seeds were still viable after a century in storage.
Without a port, the new colony was not viable.
Walking to school is viable in September but not in a January blizzard.

confused.note: Viable means workable; variable means likely to change.

questions.passage: Solar panels were long considered too costly for ordinary homes. As prices fell by ninety percent over a decade, they became a ______ alternative to power from the grid, and millions of households installed them.
questions.explanation: Falling prices made solar panels a workable option.

distractors.why: Defunct means no longer functioning, the opposite of a newly workable option.
Cynical means distrustful of motives, which does not describe a technology.
Abstract means existing only as an idea, but the panels were actually installed.

definition: to use something or someone for your own advantage, often unfairly

examples.text: Mine owners exploited child laborers until the law forbade it.
The virus exploits a weakness in the cell's outer wall.
My sister exploits the fact that I can never say no to a dare.

confused.note: Exploit means to take advantage of; explode means to burst.

questions.passage: The chess champion was quick to ______ any weakness. If an opponent left a single pawn unguarded, she would build her whole attack around it and win within twenty moves.
questions.explanation: Building an attack around an opponent's weakness is using it to her advantage.

distractors.why: Squander means to waste, the opposite of making full use of an opening.
Renounce means to give up, which she never did with an advantage.
Convey means to communicate, which does not fit.

definition: very careful, strict, and thorough

examples.text: The drug passed ten years of rigorous testing before it was approved.
Cadets followed a rigorous schedule that began at five each morning.
The lifeguard course was more rigorous than I expected, with a timed swim every day.

confused.note: Rigorous means strict and thorough; vigorous means energetic.

questions.passage: The journal is known for its ______ standards. Every article is checked by three independent experts, all data must be made public, and roughly nine submissions in ten are rejected.
questions.explanation: Triple review and a high rejection rate show strict, thorough standards.

distractors.why: Lax means loose and careless, the opposite of these standards.
Florid means overly ornate, which does not describe standards.
Cynical means distrustful, which is not the quality described.

definition: to involve something as a necessary part or result

examples.text: The experiment entails keeping the samples frozen for a year.
Building the canal entailed moving a mountain of rock.
Owning a dog entails early walks, even in the rain.

confused.note: Entail means to involve as a necessary part; a detail is a small item.

questions.passage: Applicants are often surprised to learn what the job ______. Besides teaching, a village schoolmaster was expected to ring the church bell, keep the parish records, and wind the town clock.
questions.explanation: The list of duties shows what the job necessarily involves.

distractors.why: Conveys means communicates, which does not introduce a list of duties.
Subverts means undermines, which does not fit.
Yields means produces or gives way; the sentence lists what the job requires.

definition: to waste money, time, or an opportunity carelessly

examples.text: The heir squandered in five years a fortune built over five generations.
The hero squanders his one chance to speak, and the train pulls away.
I squandered my study hall watching videos and paid for it that night.

confused.note: To squander is to waste; to wander is to roam.

questions.passage: The team led by twelve points with five minutes to play. It then ______ the advantage, missing easy shots and giving the ball away four times, and lost by one.
questions.explanation: Throwing away a large lead through careless play is wasting it.

distractors.why: Cultivated means developed and nurtured, the opposite of wasting a lead.
Exerted means applied effort or force, which does not fit "the advantage."
Conveyed means communicated or carried, which does not fit.

definition: to communicate an idea or feeling; or to carry something from one place to another

examples.text: The poem conveys grief without ever using the word.
Pipes convey water from the mountain reservoir to the city.
A thumbs-up emoji conveys a lot less enthusiasm than a phone call.

confused.note: To convey is to communicate or carry; a convoy is a group of vehicles traveling together.

questions.passage: The portrait shows the queen seated, unsmiling, with one hand resting on a closed book. Art historians believe the painter meant to ______ her seriousness and learning.
questions.explanation: The details of the portrait communicate qualities of the queen.

distractors.why: Subvert means to undermine, but the painter wished to express these qualities.
Exert means to apply force, which does not fit.
Entail means to involve necessarily, which does not describe what a painter intends to show.

partsNote: from Latin via, "road": to go along the road with

definition: something or someone that causes an important change or event to happen

examples.text: The enzyme acts as a catalyst, speeding the reaction a millionfold.
The tax on tea was the catalyst for open rebellion.
One teacher's encouragement was the catalyst for my interest in coding.

confused.note: A catalyst sets off change; an analyst studies and interprets.

questions.passage: Discontent had been building in the city for years. The ______ for the uprising, however, was a single event: the arrest of a popular baker for refusing to raise his prices.
questions.explanation: One event that set off the uprising is its trigger.

distractors.why: A deterrent discourages action, the opposite of setting off an uprising.
A propensity is a tendency, not a triggering event.
Contempt means scorn, which does not fit.

definition: believing that people act only out of self-interest; distrustful

examples.text: A cynical public assumed the reform was just another way to raise taxes.
The cynical reporter cannot believe the mayor's kindness is sincere.
I am cynical about any offer that says "free" in capital letters.

confused.note: A skeptical person wants evidence; a cynical person assumes the worst about motives.

questions.passage: Years of covering political scandals had left the reporter ______. When a senator donated her salary to charity, his first question was what she hoped to gain from the publicity.
questions.explanation: Assuming a selfish motive behind a generous act is distrust of people's motives.

distractors.why: Dispassionate means unemotional and fair, but he presumes the worst.
Florid means overly ornate, which does not fit.
Rash means hasty, which is not the trait described.

partsNote: from the Cynics, Greek philosophers who scorned convention

definition: to use power, influence, or effort to make something happen

examples.text: The moon exerts a pull on the oceans that causes the tides.
The merchants exerted great influence over the city council.
If you exert yourself on the first hill, you will have nothing left for the second.

confused.note: To exert is to apply force or effort; to exhort is to urge strongly.

questions.passage: Though she held no official position, the retired judge continued to ______ considerable influence. Younger members of the court sought her advice on nearly every difficult case.
questions.explanation: She continued to apply her influence.

distractors.why: Squander means to waste, but her influence was actively sought and used.
Renounce means to give up, but she kept her influence.
Transgress means to break a rule, which does not fit.

definition: existing only in small amounts, spread thinly over an area

examples.text: Sparse vegetation makes the plateau a difficult home for grazing animals.
The region's sparse population could not defend so long a border.
The party decorations were sparse: one balloon and a paper banner.

confused.note: Sparse means thinly scattered; spare means extra or lean.

questions.passage: Rainfall in the valley is ______, averaging less than ten centimeters a year. The few plants that survive there have deep roots and waxy leaves that hold on to every drop.
questions.explanation: Less than ten centimeters a year is very little rain.

distractors.why: Copious means abundant, the opposite of so little rain.
Rigorous means strict and thorough, which does not describe rainfall.
Viable means workable, which does not fit.

definition: no longer existing or working

examples.text: The letter was printed on the stationery of a defunct shipping company.
The defunct satellite still circles the planet as space debris.
My favorite app is now defunct, so my high scores are gone forever.

confused.note: Defunct is used for organizations, laws, and devices; extinct is the usual word for species.

questions.passage: The map shows a railway line running north from the harbor. The line is now ______: its tracks were torn up in the 1960s, and a bicycle path follows the old route.
questions.explanation: A railway whose tracks were removed no longer exists.

distractors.why: Viable means workable and alive, the opposite of a line that was torn up.
Comprehensive means all-inclusive, which does not describe a vanished railway.
Conducive means helpful toward a result, which does not fit.

partsNote: from Latin fungi, "to perform": finished performing

definition: to weaken or destroy a system, authority, or belief, especially from within

examples.text: The pamphlets were meant to subvert loyalty to the crown.
The novel subverts the reader's expectations in its final chapter.
My brother subverted the chore chart by "accidentally" erasing his name.

confused.note: To subvert is to undermine; to convert is to change into another form.

questions.passage: The playwright set out to ______ the conventions of the detective story. In her play the murderer is revealed in the first scene, and the suspense lies entirely in whether the detective will choose to arrest him.
questions.explanation: Overturning what the genre normally does undermines its conventions.

distractors.why: Uphold means to maintain, the opposite of overturning conventions.
Squander means to waste, which does not fit.
Entail means to involve necessarily, which does not fit.

definition: not influenced by strong emotion; calm and fair

examples.text: A dispassionate review of the data showed that neither side's claim held up.
The judge gave a dispassionate summary of a case that had inflamed the city.
I needed a dispassionate opinion about my essay, so I asked someone who did not know me.

confused.note: Dispassionate means calm and unemotional; compassionate means caring.

questions.passage: Both families told their stories with anger and tears. The mediator's own account was ______: she set out the facts in order, noted where the two versions differed, and offered no opinion about who was to blame.
questions.explanation: Stating facts calmly without taking sides is unemotional and fair.

distractors.why: Vehement means intensely emotional, which describes the families.
Cynical means distrustful of motives, which is not what her account shows.
Florid means overly ornate, which a plain account is not.

definition: including everything or nearly everything

examples.text: The atlas offers a comprehensive survey of the planet's ocean currents.
The treaty was the first comprehensive settlement of the border question.
The study guide is comprehensive, covering every chapter and all the labs.

confused.note: Comprehensive means complete; comprehensible means understandable.

questions.passage: Earlier guides to the region's birds described only the commonest species. The new handbook is far more ______, with an entry for every one of the 612 species ever recorded there.
questions.explanation: An entry for every recorded species covers everything.

distractors.why: Sparse means thin and scanty, the opposite of covering every species.
Comprehensible means understandable; the contrast is about completeness.
Defunct means no longer existing, which does not fit.

partsNote: from Latin prehendere, "to seize": taking in everything

definition: existing as an idea, not as a physical thing; general, not specific

examples.text: "Energy" is an abstract idea until you watch it melt a block of ice.
The poet turns abstract words like "grief" into images you can touch.
Fractions felt abstract until my teacher cut a pizza into eighths.

confused.note: Abstract means existing as an idea; obstruct means to block.

questions.passage: Young children often struggle with ______ ideas such as justice or time. Teachers therefore begin with things that can be seen and handled, such as sharing blocks fairly or watching sand run through a glass.
questions.explanation: Justice and time are ideas, not physical things.

distractors.why: Concrete means physical and specific, which describes the blocks and sand.
Defunct means no longer existing, which does not describe ideas children find hard.
Sparse means thinly scattered, which does not fit.

definition: the feeling that someone or something is worthless or deserves no respect

examples.text: The general made no secret of his contempt for politicians.
She looks at the forged painting with open contempt.
My cat regards the dog with pure contempt.

confused.note: Contempt is scorn; content means satisfied, or what something contains.

questions.passage: The veteran sailors did not trouble to hide their ______ for the new captain, who had bought his rank and had never before been to sea. They obeyed his orders slowly and mimicked his voice behind his back.
questions.explanation: Slow obedience and mockery show they think him unworthy of respect.

distractors.why: Deference means respectful submission, the opposite of mockery.
A propensity is a tendency, which does not fit "for the new captain."
A catalyst is a trigger for change, which does not fit.

definition: done too quickly, without thinking about the results

examples.text: The king's rash promise of land to both sides led straight to war.
In a rash moment he signs the contract without reading it.
It was rash to quit the team before finding out who the new coach would be.

confused.note: Rash means hasty and reckless; brash means loud and overconfident.

questions.passage: The investor later admitted that the purchase had been ______. She had bought the company after a single meeting, without visiting its factory or reading its accounts.
questions.explanation: Buying a company without checking anything is acting too quickly.

distractors.why: Rigorous means careful and thorough, the opposite of her decision.
Dispassionate means calm and unemotional, which does not describe a hasty choice.
Comprehensive means complete, which her review certainly was not.

definition: to prepare land and grow crops; or to develop a skill, quality, or relationship

examples.text: Farmers in the delta have cultivated rice for five thousand years.
The ambassador cultivated friendships at every court in Europe.
I am trying to cultivate the habit of reading before bed.

confused.note: To cultivate is to grow or develop; to captivate is to charm.

questions.passage: The diplomat understood that agreements depend on trust. Long before any negotiation began, she worked to ______ good relations with her counterparts, inviting them to dinner and remembering the names of their children.
questions.explanation: Dinners and personal attention develop relationships over time.

distractors.why: Subvert means to undermine, the opposite of building relations.
Renounce means to give up, which is not her aim.
Diminish means to lessen, but she wanted relations to grow.
